content:
I'd like to propose a method of incorporating large finite computations into Tau Ceti.

Currently, the CI is set to reject proofs with extended heartbeats, and even with extended heartbeats it can be infeasible to prove things depending on very large finite computations within the Lean kernel, or may require large computational resources. While it is important to have the ability to verify existing computations is important for formalization, not all may have resources to run such computations, and may still wish to prove theorems that depends upon such results.

While it is possible to axiomatize or prove conditional on such assumptions, that then prevents a verification challenge in knowing whether those axioms are true, which can waste valuable of time of expert reviewers. Furthermore, it can helpful for researchers to have an accessible library of completed finite computations upon which to build. Important computations include things like finite verification of the Riemann hypothesis.

This can be implemented using bounded arithmetic. That is proved to the spec of the op-codes. Certified computing or signature could be used to give a cryptographic certificate that a series of op-codes were run. This can be based on existing trusted computing paradigms, which have bene developed for machine learning and trust compilatin.

I think computations could be included in Tau Ceti through the following process:
1) Determine interesting numeric things to compute through roadmaps
2) Prove an algorithm can prove the thing you want to computation, and the possibly prove computational bounds on required computation
3) Run the computation on high powered CPU/GPU server or even cluster, perhaps using a secure enclave, which would cryptographically certify the computation was run with particular op-codes and results return. Tau Ceti could then store the cryptographic certificates of completed computations for use in proofs.
4) An axiom would be able to prove the computations result from the cryptographic signature, and could be incorporated into future Tau Ceti's proofs

I built an early prototype of some possibilities for this at https://github.com/gersh/gpu_prover/.

I'm certainly interested in exploring how to do large finite computations in Lean, but I think the "technological readiness level" here is not at the point we should be integrating this with Tau Ceti. This is stuff that needs to be worked out independently first, I think.

I only built a prototype so far. I mostly want to know what you think about:
1) Hosting a finite computation library in some form as part of Tau Ceti. Is this within scope?
2) How would you want assess whether a method of formal verification is sufficient? There are specs from CPU/GPU vendors at https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/ or https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-sdm.html. If I extract the spec, convert to a computation model in Lean, prove that a certain instruction set computes a given function, and then tell the CPU/GPU to compute something, do you trust that computation? What would be needed?

1) No, I think it is not in scope yet, because it's not something we know how to do yet.
2) I think e.g. the people working on finite computations for e.g. PNT+, #maths > Older estimates in the explicit analytic NT literature @ 💬 , etc, are the people who can start to answer whether something is sufficient.
So would you accept proofs conditional on finite computations into Tau Ceti? Would the AI reviewer get to judge whether it believes finite computation citations are legit?
No, as I said above, we should not do this in Tau Ceti.
Arklib is formalizing such proofs of knowledge
